chunks: From him, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Aban ibn Uthman, from one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

In the book of Ali (peace be upon him): 'That a prophet from the prophets complained to his Lord about judgment, saying: How can I judge with what my eye has not seen and my ear has not heard? So He said: Judge between them with clear proofs and refer them to My name, and they will swear by it.'

And he said: 'Indeed Dawud (peace be upon him) said: O Lord, show me the truth as it is with You so that I may judge by it. He said: Indeed you cannot bear that. So he persisted with his Lord until He did.'

Then a man came to him suing another man, saying: Indeed this one has taken my wealth. So God Almighty revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): 'Indeed this plaintiff killed the father of this one and took his wealth.'
So Dawud (peace be upon him) ordered that the plaintiff be killed, and his wealth was taken and given to the defendant.'
He said: 'The people were amazed and talked about it until it reached Dawud (peace be upon him), and that which he disliked entered him, so he called upon his Lord to remove that, and He did.'
Then God Almighty revealed to him: 'Judge between them with clear proofs and refer them to My name, and they will swear by it.'

key_terms.أَضِفْهُمْ إِلَى اسْمِي: refer them to My name (for oaths)
key_terms.دَاوُدَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: Prophet Dawud (David), peace be upon him

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Prophet Dawud's judgment and his complaint to God regarding legal authority?
ai.summary: This hadith, sourced from the Book of Ali (AS) in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, contrasts the limitations of human judicial perception with the divine insight granted to Prophet Dawud (AS). While Dawud was initially given the ability to see the ultimate truth—leading him to execute the plaintiff after discovering he had killed the defendant's father—God eventually guided him back to the standard legal procedure of judging by clear proofs (*bayyināt*) and oaths. This narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing intuitive justice (*hukm bi-l-haqq*) with procedural rigor (*hukm bi-l-bayyināt*) in Islamic jurisprudence. Additionally, it highlights the humility required of judges, as even a prophet with divine insight was instructed to adhere to established evidentiary standards for the sake of public understanding and legal stability.
